name: Pentapeptide-3

lead: Pentapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide name people use in anti-aging products for smoother, less lined skin. The name has referred to different peptides: before 2006 it denoted palmitoyl KTTKS (Matrixyl), and it is also tied to the Vialox brand, sold as a muscle-relaxing 'Botox-like' ingredient.

KTTKS-type peptides are described as matrikines that signal skin cells to make collagen and other matrix proteins, which is the route to firmer, smoother-looking skin. Research on the family is mostly in cultured cells, and a 2019 study of 32 KTTKS analogues found none cytotoxic to fibroblasts. Suppliers describe Vialox as reducing muscle signalling; no clinical study of a Vialox product was found.

paras: It is applied in serums and creams as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Because the name is ambiguous, users check the full ingredient name on the label to see which peptide is meant.
No adverse events were reported in the sources. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Applied for smoother, less lined skin. Depending on the peptide meant, it is described as either signalling skin cells to build collagen (the KTTKS/Matrixyl type) or relaxing muscle signalling (Vialox). Research so far is in cultured cells.

lead: Pentapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide ingredient used in topical anti-wrinkle products, where it is meant to smooth fine lines and give skin a firmer, younger-looking surface. The name is ambiguous: before 2006 the INCI name palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 referred to the Lys-Thr-Thr-Lys-Ser (KTTKS) peptide sold as Matrixyl, since renamed palmitoyl pentapeptide-4.[1][2] The ingredient sold as Vialox is also described as a pentapeptide and is marketed as a muscle-relaxing, expression-line-softening ingredient.[3]

The KTTKS family is described in the literature as matrikines, fragments of collagen that stimulate extracellular matrix production and type I and III collagen expression in cultured cells, which is the basis for their use in anti-wrinkle creams.[2][4] A 2019 study of KTTKS analogues found none cytotoxic to fibroblasts.[2]

A 2026 laboratory study evaluated Vialox and a second pentapeptide, Leuphasyl, with computer docking, molecular dynamics and a cell cytotoxicity assay. It reported that Vialox preferentially targeted SIRT-1 in the models and that neither peptide was cytotoxic to HaCaT skin cells at concentrations up to 1 mg/mL.[3]
infobox: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 is the pre-2006 INCI name for KTTKS (now pentapeptide-4)[1][2]

paras: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl) is KTTKS joined to a 16-carbon palmitoyl chain, launched by Sederma around 2000.[1] It is a matrikine, a peptide fragment thought to signal cells to produce extracellular matrix, and a 2019 paper notes it was previously labelled palmitoyl pentapeptide-3.[2][4]

Vialox is a cosmeceutical pentapeptide used in anti-aging products. A 2026 study in Chemistry & Biodiversity describes it and Leuphasyl as potential noninvasive dermocosmetic agents and examines how they bind matrix metalloproteinases (which break down collagen) and Sirtuin-1 (a regulator of cellular ageing).[3] In that work Leuphasyl interacted more strongly with MMP-13, while Vialox preferentially targeted SIRT-1, and predictions suggested favourable pharmacokinetic and safety profiles.[3]

The 2019 KTTKS analogue study found none of the tested peptides cytotoxic to fibroblasts, and three promoted cell growth.[4] The 2026 Vialox work found no cytotoxicity on HaCaT cells up to 1 mg/mL.[3]

No studies found in people for a product specified as pentapeptide-3 or Vialox. Laboratory studies of KTTKS peptides show collagen-related effects in cells; the 2019 study found palmitoylated analogues inhibited serine proteases such as plasmin and thrombin in the laboratory and did not reproduce a previously reported 150 percent collagen increase.[2][4] The 2026 Vialox work used computer modelling and a cell cytotoxicity assay.[3]

timeline.event: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 is renamed palmitoyl pentapeptide-4.[2]
A study of 32 KTTKS analogues finds them non-cytotoxic to fibroblasts.[2][4]
First combined computational and cell study of Vialox and Leuphasyl published.[3]
